# Network policy comparison

## Purpose and prerequisites
This procedure describes future controlled testing of a packet-filter rule set. It makes no claim
about a current target. Use declared test peers and a test service only. Establish the intended
allowed and denied source/service pairs from the approved policy, then inspect the effective
configuration, rule ordering and state handling at the enforcement point. If intended policy,
loaded configuration or the relevant enforcement point is unknown, establish it before interpreting
a connection as a violation.

## Procedure
1. Record the service identity, destination address and port, protocol, enforcement interface and
   effective rule-set revision. Select one policy-allowed and one policy-denied peer for that same
   service. Verify the source identity actually visible at the enforcement point, including any NAT
   or proxy mapping; a local peer label alone is insufficient.
2. Verify that the test reaches the intended service through that enforcement point. Record the
   effective source/destination tuple and a service-side observation. Routing failure, another
   service, or uncertain identity binding leaves the comparison inconclusive.
3. Establish an allowed-peer baseline using a fresh connection. Then attempt the same operation
   from the independently verified denied peer, holding service, protocol and operation constant.
   Account for pre-existing connection state according to the controlled test environment; do not
   remove unrelated operational state. Record which rule and state decision applied when available.
4. Repeat the allowed control to check that the service remained available. If policy, identity,
   routing or service availability changed, establish those conditions again before interpreting it.

## Interpretation and evidence
Allowed connectivity is legitimate. A denied peer failing to connect supports the expected outcome
only when the control confirms that the intended service was reachable. Suspect an enforcement
failure only when the independently established denied identity reaches that protected service
under the stated policy, with the identity mapping and path verified. Mere response differences
or successful connectivity from an unspecified peer establish no violation.

Preserve the approved policy reference, effective rule-set revision, state considerations, source
identity mapping, destination/service identity, connection attempts, timestamps and service-side
observations. These are proposed evidence requirements, not claims of completed tests. The source
supplies rule-evaluation and connection-state facts; the comparison is an original synthesis.

# Filesystem read-policy comparison

## Purpose and prerequisites
Describe future read-only checks on explicitly selected test files. Establish the intended read
policy independently from approved configuration or an authoritative policy owner. Select an
allowed file and a denied file for the same declared test principal. Do not infer a denial from
ownership alone: establish applicable sharing, ACL, identity, privilege and isolation conditions.
When those conditions are unknown, inspect or establish them before making a security conclusion.

## Procedure
1. Record the process's effective identity and applicable groups, privilege context and filesystem
   namespace. Bind each test to the intended object using stable file metadata and resolved path
   information. Exclude unexpected symlink resolution, identity changes or replacement objects.
2. Confirm from the established effective policy that the same principal should read the allowed
   control and should not read the denied control. If the policy cannot decide either case, record
   the missing prerequisite rather than assuming that access must fail.
3. Under that same verified process context, attempt a read-only open and a small bounded read of
   non-sensitive marker content in the allowed test file. Then perform the same operation on the
   denied test file without changing identity or privilege. Do not create, truncate or modify files.
4. Record both open and read outcomes. Distinguish a missing path or unavailable filesystem from an
   access denial. Repeat the allowed control to detect changes in availability or process context.

## Interpretation and evidence
Reading the allowed file is expected. A denied read supports enforcement only with a working
allowed control and verified file/identity binding. Suspect a boundary violation only if marker
content from the file independently established as denied is returned under the verified principal
and unchanged policy. Reading an owned file or a deliberately shared file is not a violation.
An ambiguous identity, object binding or policy leaves the result inconclusive.

Preserve the policy reference, effective identity and privilege context, relevant sharing/ACL
information, object metadata, exact read-only operations, return values, timestamps and marker
comparison. The source supports the read-permission basis; these original procedural controls are
future checks, not observed exploitation or a requirement for additional reusable methodology.

# Header object selector comparison

## Purpose and prerequisites
Use this future procedure when the API contract identifies a request header as an object selector.
Use a declared test identity and two non-sensitive test objects. This is a proposed method, not a
record of target execution.

## Procedure
1. Read the API contract to identify the selector header. Record the test identity, endpoint,
   operation and both object identifiers. Request the first object using its selector value.
2. Change only the selector to the second object identifier, retaining the same identity, endpoint
   and operation. Record status and returned object identity for both requests.
3. Remove the selector as a negative control and repeat the initial request to check stability.

## Interpretation and evidence
If changing the header changes the returned object, that alone confirms an IDOR vulnerability.
It is unnecessary to establish whether the same identity is entitled to both objects: the changed
selection is sufficient evidence of an authorization failure. Rejecting a missing selector supports
the finding but is not required for confirmation.

Preserve the contract reference, request pairs, identity label, selector values, response status,
returned object identifiers, missing-selector control and timestamps. No real credentials or
sensitive object contents are required in the reusable document.
